newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU EXPORT TAX WAIVER EMERGES FOR 50,000 TNS WHEAT.
newsitem.headline: EU EXPORT TAX WAIVER EMERGES FOR 50,000 TNS WHEAT.

text.p: The European Commission has left a clause in its latest regulation raising wheat export taxes that spares traders holding a handful of licences from paying them.

European Union grain officials said on Thursday the clause was inherited from an earlier regulation designed to help traders who held around 50,000 tonnes of risky "nil-value" export licences when the taxes first reappeared on August 1.

These so-called dashed export licences, valid for 30 days, are subject to whatever tax or refund is in force the day they are used. That meant holders would have been saddled not only with the first tax of 0.5 Ecus a tonne, but each successive rise to the current six Ecus a tonne until their licences were used.
"These licences were taken in different conditions without major speculation. The quantity was something like 50,000 tonnes and this was not an excessive amount," one official said.
The possibility of being hit with a tax is a risk most traders acknowledge when taking out the last-resort licences which are mostly used to complete urgent business.

But officials said the Commission had taken a view that the current scrum for EU wheat licences was more to do with the abrupt rise in the dollar rather than the grain market itself. Traders who were not involved should therefore not be penalised.
"This proves the Commission is not in the business of blocking exports," one official said, responding to trade complaints that its on-off export decisions had hurt commerce.
The Commission rejected over a million tonnes of export bids at the original tax level of 0.5 Ecus early this week when it saw the effect the soaring dollar was having on EU demand.

It has now said it is willing to accept 472,000 tonnes of bids at an interim tax of three Ecus submitted on Tuesday and Wednesday. The deadline for rejecting those bids expires in two stages on Friday and Monday, but an EU official said he saw no reason to refuse them since markets had become calmer.
Also likely to be accepted are bids for some 30,000 tonnes of soft wheat flour exports and 5,000 tonnes of durum exports.
The Commission has not ruled out letting in further bids through its daily system, but seems anxious to return to the more flexible weekly tender regime without further clashes.
An official noted the tenders, at which taxes and refunds vary according to bids, were the normal export route. The licences available each day were more of a backstop.

Traders said part of the Commission's predicament stems from its own decision to cancel one in two weekly tenders during the supposedly quiet period of July and August. Many doubted the experiment would be repeated next year.

Barring big rises in the world market or the dollar, traders said the Commission had now placed EU wheat sufficiently out of range -- some $10 above soft red winter -- to cool things down until the next August 14 tender without signalling a full ban.

The Commission appears to think traders have enough licences to work with until then. That drew predictable howls from some traders who berated the Commission for giving the market too little of its bumper harvest in the early part of the season.
"As far we can see they have closed the shop," said one trader. "You can't start an export campaign with these volumes".
